ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Psychiatry Consultation — Jean-Jacques Rousseau

code.originalText: Psychiatry consultation and review of the urethral imaging and cystoscopy

text.paragraph: Fixed beliefs for some nine years that former friends and colleagues are coordinating a campaign to ruin him, worse over the past year, with insomnia, in a 54-year-old writer. Please assess the diagnosis and the risk to himself and others, and advise on treatment and on his capacity to consent to urethral surgery. [S]
Urgency: Routine, within two weeks; no current suicidal or violent ideation. [S]

list.item: Is this delusional disorder, persecutory type, or does it fit paranoid personality disorder, schizophrenia, a mood disorder with psychotic features, or a medical or neurocognitive cause better? Is brain imaging needed?
What is his risk of suicide and of violence toward the people he believes are persecuting him, and is outpatient care safe?
Should an antipsychotic be offered, which one given his urinary retention, and how should it be discussed with a man who does not see himself as ill?
Is cognitive behavioral therapy for psychosis suitable, and how should we engage him without confronting the beliefs?
Does he have the capacity to consent to urethral surgery, and are there perioperative psychiatric considerations?

text.paragraph: Mr. Rousseau is seen at the request of Dr. Marchetti-Owusu. He gave a long, careful account of a campaign he believes former friends and colleagues have waged against his name for about nine years, beginning after public quarrels over his books and an attack on his previous home, and spreading in his mind to publishers, neighbors, and the staff of the house where he now lives. He believes his mail is opened and his conversations reported. He holds these beliefs with complete conviction and offers ordinary events as proof. He has never heard voices or seen things others do not, and he reports no periods of elevated mood, no sustained depression before the beliefs began, and no use of drugs. He sleeps about four hours, going over the plot at night. He works daily on his memoirs and looks after himself and his affairs. He has had no thoughts of suicide now; he recalled a passing wish to die many years ago during a painful urinary accident, without any act. He has never threatened or harmed anyone and has no wish to confront the people he fears; when afraid, his impulse is to withdraw or to move away. He agreed to the consultation for his sleep. He declined permission for collateral history. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was born in Geneva on June 28, 1712. Geneva had followed the Gregorian calendar since 1701, so the date needs no conversion. [D]
His mother, Suzanne Bernard, died nine days after his birth. [D]

In the Confessions he wrote that a defect in the bladder caused him an almost continual retention of urine in his early years; that he reached thirty almost without feeling this original infirmity, apart from frequent heats in the bladder; that burning and pain in the loins returned at Venice; and that after a hot summer of journeys on foot he had a violent nephritic colic, after which he never recovered his former health. [D]

In the Confessions he wrote that the surgeon Morand advised him to go to Daran, whose bougies were the only ones that gave him any relief; he bought a great number of them so that he would never be without, and used them often for eight or ten years. [D]

His letters show that he spoke of urinary retention from 1748, at 36. In 1761 a probe broke in his urethra and he feared it would cost him his life; he wrote that he could not stop using his probes for a single day and that he had carried a bladder disease since childhood. A surgeon, Brother Côme, succeeded in passing a probe and ruled out a stone. [D]

He described his trouble as a habitual state: he never passed urine with a full stream, the flow was never wholly stopped, and he judged that the stream grew thinner from year to year and would one day stop altogether. [D]
In 1758 he suffered frequent retentions together with a rupture, and passed the year in a state of languor that made him think he was near the end of his life. [D]
In a will dated January 29, 1763, he asked that his body be opened after death, to show that his urinary disorder did not come from a dissolute life. [D]
By his own account in the Confessions he had five children with Thérèse Levasseur, and all five were taken to the foundling hospital shortly after birth. [D]

His books were condemned in 1762; stones were thrown at his house at Môtiers in September 1765; and he came to England in January 1766 at the invitation of a Scottish philosopher. He lived at Wootton, in the parish of Ellastone in rural Staffordshire, from March 22, 1766, to May 1, 1767, in a house belonging to Richard Davenport, and wrote the first part of the Confessions there. [D]

In England he became wrongly convinced that the Scottish philosopher who had arranged his stay was at the center of a plot against him, and he feared that the servants were spying on him. The two men quarreled violently, and the 1911 Britannica called his letters of this time those of a lunatic. [D]

The French psychiatrists Sérieux and Capgras classed him among patients with a delusion of interpretation, and a 2023 history-of-medicine paper judges that by current criteria he had a paranoid delusion that appeared around the age of 45 and grew afterwards, while noting that he had real enemies and real persecution (his books condemned, and expulsion by the Swiss authorities). [R]

The cause of his urinary disorder is disputed. Proposed causes include a congenital narrowing of the urethra (Poncet and Leriche, and his own phrase, a defect of conformation), a stricture of the penile urethra (judged most probable in a 2023 paper), a muscular valve at the bladder neck (Mercier), urinary retention of psychological origin (Janet), and acute intermittent porphyria (Androutsos and Geroulanos, 2000). [R]

He distrusted the medicine of his time: in Emile he wrote that he would never call a physician for himself unless his life were in evident danger, and in the Confessions he wrote that the physicians he consulted gave him no relief and weakened him. [D]
In a letter he wrote that when snow and frost shut him in he split wood to make himself sweat twice a day, the only remedy that had ever given him the least relief. [D]

tr.td: Fixed beliefs that former friends and colleagues are plotting to ruin him, with poor sleep, present for years and worse over the past year; cause not yet established; psychiatric and medical assessment under way
S — Synthetic presenting concern at the index visit, superseded by the diagnosis at the psychiatry consultation; his documented beliefs of 1766 are echoed.

Weak urinary stream, straining, incomplete emptying (post-void residual 180 mL), and painful urination since childhood, treated for years by self-dilation with urethral sounds; cause not yet established; urethral imaging and endoscopy booked
S — Synthetic presenting concern at the index visit, superseded by the urethrogram and cystoscopy diagnosis; his documented lifelong retention and self-treatment with bougies are echoed.

Delusional disorder, persecutory type (DSM-5-TR), of about nine years' duration, with non-bizarre beliefs of a coordinated campaign against him; no hallucinations, disorganization, or mood episode; normal cognition; insomnia secondary to preoccupation; synthetic modern counterpart of his documented persecutory beliefs
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis. His beliefs and conduct are documented (D); calling them a paranoid delusion is a retrospective interpretation (R), made difficult by the real persecution he suffered.

Bulbar urethral stricture, 1.5 cm, dense and ring-like (lumen about 8 French), idiopathic and probably congenital in origin, with decades of self-dilation; bladder trabeculation without hydronephrosis; kidney function normal; synthetic modern counterpart of his documented lifelong urinary retention

S — Synthetic modern diagnosis. His lifelong retention is documented (D); its cause is disputed (R), and the autopsy found no urethral lesion (D), so this stricture is not presented as his historical diagnosis.
Right inguinal hernia, reducible and minimally symptomatic, likely aggravated by years of straining to pass urine
S — Synthetic finding on examination; it echoes the documented rupture of 1758, whose site the source does not state.

tr.td: Tired, neatly dressed, courteous, initially guarded, warmer as the interview went on

Alert and oriented; speech fluent, faster on the theme of the plot; mood "worn out"; affect anxious; thought process logical and detailed; fixed, non-bizarre persecutory beliefs held with full conviction; no hallucinations; no passivity experiences or thought interference; no suicidal or violent ideation, intent, or plan; insight into the beliefs absent; judgment intact for his own care
Attention, memory, and language intact in conversation, consistent with MoCA 28
No tremor, rigidity, or abnormal movements

text.paragraph: No results recorded at this visit.

list.item: Delusional disorder, persecutory type (DSM-5-TR) (F22). Non-bizarre persecutory delusions for well over a month (about nine years), with function preserved apart from the effects of the beliefs, and no hallucinations, disorganization, or negative symptoms, so the criteria for schizophrenia are not met. Paranoid personality disorder describes pervasive suspicious attitudes held as attitudes; his beliefs are fixed, specific, and unshaken by contrary evidence, which makes them delusions, although long-standing sensitive and suspicious traits may have preceded them. The mild depressive and anxious symptoms followed the beliefs and are not a mood episode with psychotic features. A normal neurological examination, MoCA 28, normal laboratory tests, no substance use, and a long, stable course make a medical or neurocognitive cause unlikely, so brain imaging is not needed now; it would be if cognition declined, neurological signs appeared, or the course changed. The beliefs grew from real conflicts, which should be acknowledged rather than dismissed. [S]

Risk. Low risk of suicide and of violence at present: no current ideation, no history of violence, no wish to confront anyone, no weapons, and no substance misuse. The risks to watch are sudden flight from his home, isolation, insomnia, and any shift toward wanting to confront someone. Outpatient care is safe. [S]

Antipsychotic medication. An antipsychotic often reduces the distress and preoccupation of delusional disorder, though the beliefs may persist. Aripiprazole 5 mg is the best choice for him: it has almost no anticholinergic effect, so it will not worsen urinary retention, and it causes little sedation, weight gain, or prolactin rise. Drugs with marked anticholinergic effects, such as olanzapine, quetiapine, or the low-potency first-generation drugs, should be avoided. I offered it framed around his own goals of sleep and peace of mind; he declined today, which he is entitled to do, and it should be offered again. [S]

Psychological treatment and engagement. He is suitable for cognitive behavioral therapy for psychosis aimed at distress, worry, sleep, and safety behaviors rather than at the truth of the beliefs. He accepted it. Engagement depends on not arguing with or colluding in the beliefs, acknowledging his real grievances, keeping promises, and letting him read his records. [S]

Capacity and the operation. He understands and retains information about his urinary condition and its treatment, appreciates that it applies to him, weighs the options, and communicates a choice. His beliefs do not involve his doctors or the operation. He has capacity for this decision, and the delusional disorder is not a reason to doubt it. Perioperative risk of delirium is low; avoid benzodiazepines and anticholinergic drugs, and keep his routines and written information. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Marchetti-Owusu's referral and examination; MoCA 28; PHQ-9 8 with item 9 scored 0; GAD-7 9; blood count, metabolic panel, calcium, TSH, and vitamin B12, all normal; the kidney and bladder ultrasound and the urethrogram and cystoscopy reports from five days ago, which show a 1.5 cm bulbar urethral stricture. [S]

list.item: Diagnosis: delusional disorder, persecutory type; no brain imaging now. [S]
Cognitive behavioral therapy for psychosis, about 16 sessions with the clinic psychologist, starting next week. [S]

Offer aripiprazole 5 mg each morning again at later visits; if he starts it, obtain baseline weight, waist, blood pressure, fasting glucose or hemoglobin A1c, lipids, and AIMS, and follow the monitoring schedule; avoid strongly anticholinergic antipsychotics. [S]
Sleep: fixed rising time and daylight activity; no sedating antihistamines, benzodiazepines, or other anticholinergic sleep aids. [S]

Review suicide and violence risk at every visit and keep the safety plan and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline current; seek urgent review if he wants to confront someone, stops sleeping, or plans to leave his home suddenly. [S]
He has capacity to consent to urethral surgery; proceed with whatever he chooses after the urology discussion. [S]
Give him copies of his notes and results, and keep the same clinicians where possible. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Marchetti-Owusu the same day. Mr. Rousseau was given a written summary of the diagnosis as "a condition that can make worries about other people fixed and exhausting" and of the options, and agreed to start the therapy. [S]

Follow-up: Primary care continues the visits, measurement, and safety review, and may start aripiprazole whenever he chooses it without waiting for a psychiatry appointment. Psychiatry will see him again if he asks, if the risk changes, or if there is little response after twelve weeks of medication. [S]
